reference.source: Nelson Textbook of Pediatrics / Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine
clinicalPearls: A major cause of primary (congenital) lactic acidosis, resulting from deficient activity of the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex that links glycolysis to the citric acid cycle
The most common form is due to X-linked mutations in the E1-alpha subunit (PDHA1), so both males and females can be affected
Presentations range from severe neonatal lactic acidosis to progressive neurological disease with developmental delay, hypotonia, seizures and episodic ataxia

A characteristic feature is that lactate rises rather than falls after carbohydrate intake, and the blood lactate-to-pyruvate ratio is typically normal (in contrast to respiratory chain defects where it is high)
Structural brain abnormalities such as corpus callosum agenesis, and a Leigh syndrome pattern of basal ganglia and brainstem lesions, may be present
Because glucose cannot be used efficiently, a ketogenic (high-fat, low-carbohydrate) diet is a central management principle, providing an alternative fuel that bypasses the block
Thiamine (a cofactor of the complex) is supplemented and may benefit thiamine-responsive variants; dichloroacetate has been used to lower lactate
Not a standard target of newborn screening, so diagnosis rests on recognising congenital lactic acidosis and neurological features and confirming enzymatically or genetically
reference.pathophysiology: The pyruvate dehydrogenase complex converts pyruvate, the end product of glycolysis, into acetyl-CoA, linking carbohydrate metabolism to the citric acid cycle and oxidative energy production. When the complex is deficient, pyruvate cannot enter the cycle and is instead diverted to lactate and alanine, producing lactic acidosis with a normal lactate-to-pyruvate ratio. The brain, which depends heavily on glucose oxidation for energy, is particularly affected, resulting in structural malformations, neurodegeneration and a Leigh-like phenotype. Providing fat-derived ketones and acetyl-CoA through a ketogenic diet bypasses the enzymatic block and supplies the brain with usable fuel.
additionalDifferentials: Mitochondrial respiratory chain disorders (high lactate-to-pyruvate ratio)
Organic acidaemias and other causes of lactic acidosis
Leigh syndrome of other genetic cause
additionalInvestigations: Blood and CSF lactate and pyruvate with a normal lactate-to-pyruvate ratio
Neuroimaging for corpus callosum abnormalities and Leigh-pattern lesions
Enzyme assay of the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex in fibroblasts or leukocytes
Molecular testing including the X-linked PDHA1 gene
Assessment of the lactate response to a carbohydrate load
redFlags: Severe neonatal lactic acidosis with encephalopathy is a metabolic emergency
Acute worsening of lactic acidosis and neurological function after carbohydrate loading
Rapidly progressive encephalopathy or brainstem involvement in a Leigh-syndrome presentation
Intractable seizures or apnoea in the neonatal period
reference.prognosis: Prognosis is generally guarded and correlates with the severity of residual enzyme activity; severe neonatal forms often have a poor outcome, whereas milder and thiamine-responsive variants and early ketogenic dietary treatment can improve neurological outcome, though the disorder is not curable.
pitfalls: Loading a hypotonic, acidotic infant with intravenous glucose, which can worsen lactic acidosis
Confusing it with respiratory chain disease by not checking the lactate-to-pyruvate ratio
Missing affected females because the common defect is X-linked
management: Institute a ketogenic, high-fat, low-carbohydrate diet as a central therapy, supplying ketones that bypass the enzymatic block and fuel the brain
Trial thiamine, a cofactor of the complex, since some variants are thiamine-responsive
Avoid carbohydrate loading, which paradoxically worsens the lactic acidosis
In acute lactic acidosis provide supportive correction and consider dichloroacetate to lower lactate by inhibiting pyruvate dehydrogenase kinase
Provide anticonvulsants for seizures and developmental, physiotherapy and occupational support for the neurological impairment
Monitor blood lactate, growth and neurodevelopment through a metabolic and neurology team
Offer genetic counselling and family screening, noting the X-linked PDHA1 inheritance of the commonest form
